questions.question: Why is an empirical study needed after code testing in interactive system development?
options: To confirm that all unit, integration, and system tests have passed
To verify that the system is executable after unit and integration testing
To replace the design-prototype-evaluate cycle once a stable interface is reached
To estimate usability, which code testing does not show.
questions.explanation: Code testing can show that the system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable, so usability testing or an empirical study is needed to estimate usability.

questions.question: What rule in the traditional interactive system development lifecycle can lead to time and cost overruns?
options: Completing every activity and requirement in a stage before starting the next stage.
Starting deployment after every successful interface prototype
Removing unnecessary documentation from the project
Delivering usable features in short successive sprints
questions.explanation: The traditional lifecycle is rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts, and this strict stage completion can lead to time and cost overruns.

questions.question: Why can a stage in the standard interactive system development lifecycle take longer than the stage's actual work?
options: Because every prototype must be rebuilt after each code review
Because sensor orientation must be re-registered for each stage
Because documentation for the stage must also be prepared.
Because new participants must be found for every stage
questions.explanation: Each stage requires a long time not only because of executing the stage but also because documentation for the stage must be prepared.

questions.question: When is the interface design-prototype-evaluate cycle complete in interactive system development?
options: When the interface design is stable and further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.
When the first prototype passes a cognitive walkthrough
When the client signs the software requirement specification
When all code units have passed system-level testing
questions.explanation: The cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

questions.question: In interactive system development, from whom do usability requirements primarily come?
options: End users.
Both clients and end users equally
The development team's design guidelines
Clients
questions.explanation: Usability requirements primarily come from end users, while other non-functional requirements may come from clients and functional requirements may come from both.

questions.question: How does agile development differ from the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle in delivery?
options: It delivers the system only after all stage documents are prepared
It delivers usable features over successive deliveries
It delivers a finished system only after all requirements are collected
It completes the whole system before making the first delivery
questions.explanation: Agile development keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, whereas the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle first completes the system and then delivers it.

questions.question: Which sequence best represents the work inside an agile sprint?
options: Testing, development, requirements from stakeholder feedback, then delivery to production
Requirements from the product sprint backlog and feedback, development, testing with training and documentation, then delivery to production
Development, requirements from the product sprint backlog, testing, then deployment after all documentation is approved
Requirements, deployment to production, development, then testing and training
questions.explanation: An agile sprint includes requirements based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development, then testing including training and documentation, and then delivery to production.

questions.question: Which practice in agile development lets the team address stakeholder needs quickly during sprints?
options: Waiting until the end of the project to collect customer comments
Complete documentation of every stage before any feedback is shared
Live demonstrations after iterations and quick feedback shared before the next sprint
A final usability study after all coding is completed
questions.explanation: The development team provides a live demonstration after each iteration and regularly collects quick feedback from stakeholders and customers, which is shared with the team before the next sprint so it can be addressed.

questions.question: Why does agile development avoid trying to do everything from the beginning?
options: To test the whole system only after all features are coded
To eliminate unnecessary elements and documentation and achieve a quick, client-acceptable turnaround
To identify every end-user requirement before a sprint starts
To complete all requirements and documentation before development starts
questions.explanation: Agile development starts small, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, and eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation to ensure a quick project turnaround.

questions.question: In contrast to agile methods, what is the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle primarily meant for?
options: Delivering short sprints with live demonstrations
Understanding the overall development flow for pedagogical purposes
Building practical systems within a reasonable time frame
Collecting quick customer feedback before every development step
questions.explanation: The Interactive System Development Life Cycle is primarily meant for understanding the overall flow and for pedagogical purposes, rather than for building practical systems within a reasonable time frame.

questions.question: How do the sources of requirements in the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development compare with the way requirements are formed in an agile sprint?
questions.reference_answer: In the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development, functional requirements may come from both clients and end users, usability requirements primarily come from end users, and other non-functional requirements may come from clients. In an agile sprint, requirements are based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback. Quick feedback from stakeholders and customers is collected regularly and shared with the team before the next sprint.

questions.question: Why can deployment in an interactive system development lifecycle take a very long time?
questions.reference_answer: The interactive system development lifecycle can be rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts and before deployment. Deployment is reached only after requirement gathering, coding, code testing, and usability testing, and each stage also needs time for documentation. Before deployment, it requires a feasibility study report, a software requirements specification, design documents, a code testing document, and a usability study report.

questions.question: Why is code testing not enough to establish that an interactive system is usable, and how does empirical study fit with earlier prototype evaluation?
questions.reference_answer: Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable, so an empirical study is needed to estimate usability. In the iterative software development life cycle, early evaluation in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code testing, and empirical study are the evaluation points. Early quick evaluation can use cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation to inspect a prototype and identify usability problems.

questions.question: How does agile development keep delivering value without first developing the entire interactive system?
questions.reference_answer: Agile development starts small and does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning. It keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries. In a sprint, requirements come from the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, followed by testing including training and documentation and delivery to production, while daily meetings or brainstorming, demonstrations, and quick feedback keep the team able to change quickly.
